strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: improving conditional coverage and disentangling/calibrating aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in regression.
The proposed CLEAR framework is simple and modular: it introduces two calibration parameters, gamma1 and lambda, and is compatible with arbitrary aleatoric and epistemic estimators.
The residual-based quantile regression for aleatoric uncertainty is sensible and appears to improve stability over direct target quantile regression, especially under underfitting.

The empirical evaluation is relatively extensive: 17 real-world tabular datasets, synthetic simulations, multiple metrics (PICP, NIW, NCIW, quantile loss, AISL), multiple CLEAR variants, and a case study.
The method shows practical gains over PCS and standard/ALEATORIC CQR baselines in interval width and quantile loss while approximately maintaining nominal coverage on the reported benchmarks.
The paper includes theoretical discussion, including an asymptotic conditional-coverage lemma and a finite-sample marginal-coverage result for a modified Conformalized CLEAR procedure.
The adaptive lambda parameter provides useful interpretability about whether aleatoric or epistemic uncertainty dominates in a given dataset or region.
weaknesses: The main CLEAR algorithm reuses the validation set for model selection, lambda tuning, and conformal calibration, which breaks the standard exchangeability assumptions and thus does not provide finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees. The finite-sample guarantee is only for a modified split procedure not used in the main experiments.

The methodological novelty is incremental: combining aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty with tunable weights has been explored in prior work (e.g., UACQR and Bayesian/ensemble approaches). The two-parameter calibration is natural but not a fundamental advance, and some 'first' claims appear overstated.

The improvement over the strongest baseline, ALEATORIC-R, is modest (about 3% NCIW and 9.4% quantile loss). Much of the gain may come from the residual-based aleatoric modeling rather than from the two-parameter calibration itself.

The baseline suite is limited in the main paper: mostly CQR/PCS variants and the authors' own improved ALEATORIC-R. There is no main-text comparison to modern UQ methods such as deep ensembles, MC dropout, Bayesian neural networks, Gaussian processes, NOMU, or a broader set of conformal methods. UACQR is only compared in an appendix.

Lambda is selected by optimizing quantile loss on the same data later used for calibration, using a very dense grid (over 4000 values). This can overfit, especially on smaller datasets, and the paper does not provide a systematic sensitivity or overfitting analysis.

The asymptotic conditional-coverage result relies on strong assumptions: consistency of the PCS ensemble and the quantile regression estimators. For finite bootstrap ensembles with model selection, these consistency assumptions may be difficult to justify, and the proof is only sketched.

The evaluation is restricted to tabular regression. Despite claims of broad applicability, there is no evidence for classification, time series, high-dimensional/image data, or large-scale deep-learning settings.
Reproducibility is not fully addressed: no explicit release of CLEAR code is mentioned, and some implementation details are buried in dense appendices with notation inconsistencies.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: combining aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty for calibrated prediction intervals.
The proposed CLEAR method is simple, modular, and compatible with existing aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimators.
The empirical study is relatively extensive, covering 17 tabular regression datasets, multiple metrics, synthetic simulations, and a case study.
The paper includes useful ablations (variants a/b/c, fixed lambda, fixed gamma1) and discusses reproducibility details such as model choices and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: CLEAR essentially learns two scaling parameters for an existing additive combination of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Many Bayesian/ensemble methods already combine these components, and related conformal work such as UACQR already tunes one of the two parameters. The repeated 'first' claims are overstatements.

The theoretical support is weak for the actual algorithm. Lemma 2.1 is nearly trivial and does not validate the method: if the epistemic estimator is consistent, its contribution vanishes asymptotically, making lambda irrelevant in the limit. The proof ignores model selection, bootstrap ensembles, finite-sample effects, and validation-based lambda selection.

The actual CLEAR procedure does not have finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees. The authors admit that reusing the validation set as the calibration set and optimizing two parameters invalidates standard conformal guarantees. Their proposed Conformalized CLEAR variant is not used or evaluated in the main experiments.

Evaluation is not sufficiently competitive for a top-tier AI venue. The main baselines are largely the authors' own components or improved variants (CQR, ALEATORIC-R, PCS). Strong modern uncertainty-quantification baselines such as deep ensembles, MC dropout, Bayesian neural networks, Gaussian processes, NOMU, and UACQR are missing from the main paper; UACQR appears only in the appendix and sometimes outperforms CLEAR.

The headline improvements are partly against weaker self-calibrated baselines. Against the strongest baseline (ALEATORIC-R), the main variant improves NCIW by only about 3% and quantile loss by about 9.4%. CLEAR is not consistently best across all datasets.

The method uses the same validation set for model selection, lambda selection, and conformal calibration, which can overfit the validation set and inflate apparent performance, especially on small datasets. The NCIW metric also uses test-time recalibration, which may obscure miscalibration and makes width comparisons harder to interpret.

The interpretation of PCS ensemble variability as epistemic uncertainty is heuristic rather than theoretically grounded, and the residual-based quantile regression may not produce valid conditional quantiles under model misspecification or complex heteroskedasticity.

Positioning and clarity suffer from overclaiming and some notational/implementation ambiguities. The contribution is incremental relative to existing uncertainty decomposition and conformal calibration work.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: combining aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty for calibrated prediction intervals.

Proposes a simple and general two-parameter calibration scheme (gamma1, lambda) that is compatible with arbitrary aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimators and enables adaptive, data-driven weighting.

Provides a thorough empirical evaluation on 17 real-world tabular regression datasets across 10 seeds, multiple metrics, three model variants, and a case study, generally maintaining nominal coverage while reducing interval width and quantile loss relative to core baselines.
The residual-based aleatoric estimator and the combination of PCS ensembles with CQR are reasonable practical contributions that improve stability over direct target quantile fitting.
Includes an asymptotic conditional-coverage argument and a finite-sample conformal variant in the appendix, with useful discussion of limitations and interpretation of lambda.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest: the main idea is to tune scaling and the ratio between existing aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty components, which is an incremental calibration wrapper rather than a fundamentally new uncertainty quantification framework.

The default CLEAR procedure reuses the validation set for lambda selection and conformal calibration, so it lacks finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees. The theoretical finite-sample version (Conformalized CLEAR) requires a separate calibration split and is not empirically evaluated in the main experiments.

The fast conformity-score implementation in Appendix B appears off by one if interpreted literally: the score uses (l~ - y)/(f - l~) and (y - u~)/(u~ - f), but the final interval scales by gamma1 without an apparent +1 correction. This raises calibration-correctness concerns and needs clarification.

Baselines are mostly restricted to CQR/PCS variants and the authors' own improved CQR versions; broader uncertainty quantification baselines such as deep ensembles, MC dropout, Bayesian neural networks, and Gaussian processes are largely absent, with UACQR only in the appendix.

Improvement over the strongest baseline (ALEATORIC-R) is relatively small in several metrics (e.g., about 3% NCIW and 9.4% quantile loss), while the abstract emphasizes larger improvements over weaker individually calibrated baselines.

Using a dense grid of over 4000 lambda values on small validation/calibration sets may overfit the validation metric; the paper acknowledges this but provides limited sensitivity or robustness analysis.

Some 'first' claims are potentially overstated, and the empirical scope is limited to tabular regression, with no classification, time-series, or large-scale deep-learning experiments despite future-work discussion.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: combining epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty for calibrated regression intervals.
Proposes a simple, modular calibration scheme with two parameters (gamma1, lambda) that can be applied on top of different uncertainty estimators.
Provides extensive empirical evaluation across 17 real-world datasets, synthetic simulations, multiple CLEAR variants, deep ensembles/SQR combinations, and conformalized settings.
The residual-based quantile regression component for aleatoric uncertainty is sensible and appears to improve stability over direct quantile regression on targets.
Includes useful appendices with implementation details, ablations, runtime analysis, and some theoretical discussion.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: combining/scaling aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties is already explored, and the main new element—tuning the mixing ratio lambda and scale gamma1 via validation quantile loss—is incremental relative to existing approaches such as UACQR.

Main experiments do not directly compare against the closest method, UACQR, and the largest improvements are against weaker individual baselines; gains over the strongest internal baseline (ALEATORIC-R) are modest (roughly 3% NCIW and 9% quantile loss).
Fixed alternatives such as lambda=1 or gamma1=1 often perform nearly as well in the appendix, which weakens the central claim that adaptively learning both parameters is necessary.

The standard experimental setup reuses the same validation data for both lambda selection and conformal calibration of gamma1, so the finite-sample coverage guarantees do not apply; the conformalized version is only in the appendix.

The theoretical support is not fully convincing: the asymptotic lemma relies on strong/possibly incorrect consistency assumptions, and if epistemic uncertainty vanishes asymptotically, CLEAR essentially reduces to the aleatoric quantile estimator.

Conditional coverage is demonstrated mainly in simulations, while real-data evaluation focuses on marginal coverage and interval-width metrics; no image, time-series, or large-scale non-tabular benchmarks are included.
Some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially abstract-level improvement numbers that compare against selected weaker baselines rather than the strongest available alternatives.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: uncertainty quantification and combining aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty for regression prediction intervals.
The proposed CLEAR method is simple, modular, and compatible with different base uncertainty estimators, including PCS/CQR and deep ensembles/SQR.
The empirical evaluation is broad: 17 real-world datasets, multiple random splits, simulations, several metrics, a case study, and runtime analysis.
The paper is generally clear in its algorithm description and provides substantial appendix details, hyperparameters, and implementation information.
The method shows consistent empirical improvements over several component baselines while maintaining approximately nominal coverage on the reported benchmarks.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and incremental: the core contribution is essentially learning two scalar calibration weights for existing aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates. The closest prior work, UACQR, is conceptually very similar and is not included as a main-table baseline.

The main 'standard' experimental configuration reuses the validation set as the calibration set and selects lambda on the same data used to calibrate gamma1, which invalidates the usual split-conformal finite-sample coverage guarantee. The conformalized version with a separate calibration split is only in the appendix and is not the main method.

The theoretical contribution is weak. Lemma 2.1 only provides asymptotic conditional validity under strong consistency assumptions, and in that limit the epistemic quantile spread vanishes, so the result largely reduces to assuming a consistent aleatoric quantile estimator. It does not justify the finite-sample behavior or the role of lambda/gamma2.

The aleatoric/epistemic decomposition is not rigorously identified. Training quantile regression on residuals from a PCS point predictor may absorb epistemic bias into what is labeled aleatoric uncertainty, making the semantic interpretation questionable.

The evaluation lacks several important comparisons in the main paper. In particular, UACQR, the closest method, appears only in the appendix and only for one variant, while the main results compare mainly against the paper's own component baselines.
Quantile loss is used both to select lambda and as a primary evaluation metric, which risks favoring the proposed method and weakens the objectivity of the reported gains.
The lambda grid is extremely large (over 4000 values) and optimized on validation data, which can overfit, especially for smaller datasets or smaller calibration/validation splits.

The paper overstates its novelty with repeated 'first' claims. Prior work already combines epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty and applies calibration; the specific choice to learn both gamma1 and lambda is a useful but relatively small technical variation.

Real-world evaluation focuses on marginal interval metrics and average widths rather than conditional coverage. The claimed improvements in conditional coverage are demonstrated mainly in simulations, not thoroughly on the real datasets.

The empirical gains may be sensitive to base model choice, calibration split reuse, and implementation details, and the main paper does not sufficiently isolate how much comes from lambda selection versus gamma1 calibration.

strengths: Addresses an important uncertainty-quantification problem: calibrating and combining aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty to improve conditional coverage and interval sharpness.
The CLEAR framework is simple, modular, and compatible with any pair of aleatoric and epistemic estimators; the adaptive weighting via lambda is intuitive and data-driven.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: synthetic simulations, 17 real-world regression datasets, multiple metrics, three CLEAR variants, and additional experiments with Deep Ensembles and Simultaneous Quantile Regression.

The paper provides a conformalized variant with finite-sample marginal coverage and an asymptotic conditional-coverage result, plus detailed appendices on implementation, metrics, runtime, and a case study.
Results show consistent improvements over the individual calibrated components and strong performance across many datasets, supporting the practical usefulness of the approach.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior work such as UACQR, which already tunes the aleatoric/epistemic ratio with gamma1 fixed. The main addition is calibrating gamma1 as well, so claims of being the first to introduce two calibration parameters are somewhat overstated.

The default CLEAR algorithm reuses the validation set for calibration, so it does not inherit standard finite-sample conformal coverage guarantees. The conformalized version is relegated to the appendix, while the main experiments use the unguaranteed default.

The theoretical result is asymptotic and relies on consistency of the base estimators. It does not address finite-sample behavior, lambda-selection variance, or overfitting of gamma1/lambda on small calibration sets.
The closest external baseline, UACQR, is only compared in the appendix rather than in the main experimental tables, weakening the central empirical positioning.

Quantile loss is used both to select lambda and as a main evaluation metric, which may introduce optimistic bias. NCIW is computed after test-time recalibration, which can obscure absolute calibration issues, although PICP is also reported.
Reproducibility would be stronger with an explicit code release or artifact; the appendix is detailed but the paper does not mention public code.
